conceptCards.title: Union types (A | B) and exhaustiveness
conceptCards.summary: A union type says a value can be one of several shapes — like a function parameter that accepts either a string or a number.

conceptCards.title: Intersection types (A & B) and mixing shapes
conceptCards.summary: An intersection type merges multiple type descriptions into one value that must satisfy all of them at once — like a user who is both an employee and a manager.

conceptCards.title: Type widening, narrowing, and control flow
conceptCards.summary: TypeScript starts with a precise type and sometimes broadens it on purpose — or narrows it when your `if` checks prove which branch you are in.

conceptCards.title: Assignability, subtyping, and excess property checks
conceptCards.summary: TypeScript decides whether one type can stand in for another using structural rules — if the shape fits, the assignment works.
conceptCards.example: type Point = { x: number; y: number };

conceptCards.title: Discriminated unions and tagged unions
conceptCards.summary: When each variant carries a shared tag field like `kind` or `type`, TypeScript follows that tag and unlocks the right fields automatically.

conceptCards.title: readonly, Readonly<T>, and immutability flags
conceptCards.summary: The readonly keyword tells TypeScript that a property or array should not be mutated after creation — a compile-time promise, not a runtime lock.

conceptCards.title: Index signatures and Record<K, V>
conceptCards.summary: An index signature types dynamic string keys on an object — like a dictionary of HTTP headers or translation strings.

conceptCards.title: TypeScript structural types versus C# nominal types
conceptCards.summary: TypeScript checks shape, not names — if two types have the same properties, they are compatible.
conceptCards.example: interface User { id: string; name: string; }
